source: Casasanto (2016) A shared mechanism of linguistic, cultural, and bodily relativity (Language Learning 66(3):714-730)
finding: Abstract only (via Crossref). Casasanto argues that language is not special: linguistic, cultural and bodily experience all shape thought by strengthening some implicit associations in long-term memory and weakening others. This is the continuity (shared mechanism) view. It is a close sibling of the Routledge Handbook chapter named in the brief, not the chapter itself.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract. Crossref lists 26 citations. Full text not opened (publisher page returned HTTP 403, PDF fetch returned an HTML wall).
quote: What's special about the way language influences thought? In some cases, the answer may be: nothing at all.
limits: The abstract does not say which individual Whorfian effects he thinks are robust, and it does not use the labels Deep View or Shallow View. The Routledge chapter (a22) remains unread.
agent_relevance: Supports reading wording effects as habit-strengthened associations, not as a fixed language filter. Background only.

source: Chen (2007) Do Chinese and English speakers think about time differently? Failure of replicating Boroditsky (2001), Cognition 104(2)
finding: Secondary summary only (WebSearch result text and Miles et al. 2011 intro). Chen ran the same priming paradigm and found no reliable reaction-time difference between horizontal and vertical spatial primes in Chinese or English speakers. A corpus count showed Chinese uses horizontal metaphors for time more often than vertical ones, so the premise of the original claim was also doubted.
numbers: Sample sizes and test statistics NOT recovered: the Cognition paper is paywalled and the abstract text in OpenAlex is empty. Miles et al. 2011 (d05) call the attempts by Chen and by January and Kako 'largely unsuccessful'.
limits: Gap 4 stays open for the exact N and effect sizes. Do not quote any figure for this study.
agent_relevance: None directly. Reminder that one famous priming result did not travel.

source: January and Kako (2007) Re-evaluating evidence for linguistic relativity: Reply to Boroditsky (2001), Cognition 104(2)
finding: Known only through the abstract of Tse and Altarriba (2008): January and Kako ran six experiments on English monolinguals and did not reproduce Boroditsky's finding that English speakers are faster after a horizontal than a vertical prime.
numbers: Six experiments (count from the Tse and Altarriba abstract). Per-experiment N and statistics not recovered; OpenAlex abstract empty.
limits: Second-hand. The 'six experiments' figure is the one new fact for gap 4.
agent_relevance: Same as d02.

source: Tse and Altarriba (2008) Evidence against linguistic relativity in Chinese and English: a case study of spatial and temporal metaphors, J Cognition and Culture 8
finding: Abstract read via OpenAlex. They failed to replicate the English-monolingual half: both English monolinguals and Chinese-English bilinguals verified temporal sentences faster after a vertical than a horizontal prime. They say they partly replicated the bilingual half. Because both groups looked the same, they argue against linguistic relativity.
numbers: No N or statistics in the abstract. Pattern: same direction (vertical-prime advantage) in both groups.
limits: Abstract only. The bilingual result was a partial replication, so the three 'failed replications' are not equally clean failures. Boroditsky's English-speaker half failed twice (January and Kako, Tse and Altarriba).
agent_relevance: None directly.

source: Miles, Tan, Noble, Lumsden, Macrae (2011) Can a mind have two time lines? Mandarin and English speakers, Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 18:598-604
finding: Exp 1 (image classification with keypad responses): Mandarin-English bilinguals responded faster on compatible than incompatible trials in both horizontal and vertical orientations; English monolinguals showed an orientation x trial-type interaction. Exp 2: sequence photos of a Chinese actor biased bilinguals toward vertical ordering, photos of an American actor toward horizontal. The paper notes earlier attempts to corroborate Boroditsky (Chen 2007; January and Kako 2007) were 'largely unsuccessful'.
numbers: Exp 1: three-way group x orientation x trial type F(1,42)=4.90, p<.05, partial eta2=.10. Bilinguals (N about 25, df 24): compatible 736 ms vs incompatible 772 ms; trial type F(1,24)=5.76, partial eta2=.19; no orientation interaction (F<0.5). English (N about 19, df 18): orientation x trial type F(1,18)=5.07, partial eta2=.22. Group sizes inferred from degrees of freedom.
limits: Small groups. Findings depend on cultural context cues. Supports flexible, context-triggered timelines but not a fixed language effect.
agent_relevance: Context cues can switch the frame a speaker uses, so an LLM's frame choice may also depend on cheap cues in the prompt (untested).

source: Chen and O'Seaghdha (2013) Do Mandarin and English speakers think about time differently? Review of existing evidence and some new data
finding: Per a search summary: the review concludes the evidence is weak that Mandarin and English speakers think about time in a categorically different way because their spatial time metaphors differ. Chen et al. 2011 found Taiwanese Mandarin speakers showed the opposite pattern to mainland Chinese, who matched English speakers, and tied it to writing direction.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Second-hand (search snippet).
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Language and economic behaviour: Future tense use causes less not more temporal discounting (PLOS ONE 20(5), 2025), Study 1
finding: Study 1 elicited English and Dutch speakers' future-tense use, then measured intertemporal choice. Mediation tested whether habitual future-tense use raises discounting, as the Chen (2013) temporal hypothesis predicts. Among English speakers, more future-tense use went with LESS discounting, the opposite of the hypothesis.
numbers: Final N=235 (113 English, 122 Dutch) from 240 recruited; Bayesian mediation, posterior credibility intervals. Data collected Jan-Feb 2017 (Oxford and MPI). Power analysis targeted N>228.
limits: Correlational mediation, two languages only. Authors propose certainty (modal) semantics instead of temporal distance. Author names not captured in this session.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that the FTR to patience mechanism behind Goli and Singh is itself contested, so an LLM FTR gap cannot be read as a Whorfian effect.

source: Language and economic behaviour: Future tense use causes less not more temporal discounting (PLOS ONE 2025), Study 2
finding: Study 2 repeated Study 1 with a larger sample and again found that higher future-tense use in English predicted less, not more, discounting. The authors conclude obligatory future tense is not responsible for the cross-cultural FTR correlations and suggest low-certainty modals (may, might) may matter instead.
numbers: Final N=606 (301 English from Prolific, 305 Dutch from Qualtrics) from 625; 7 excluded for bad faith, 12 for a survey error.
limits: Two languages. Online choice task.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 asks whether the Goli and Singh LLM effect replicates; this paper says the human mechanism under it does not replicate in this test.

source: Search note: independent replications of Goli and Singh (2024) 'Can LLMs capture human preferences? / Language, time preferences, and consumer behavior' (arXiv 2305.02531)
finding: Searches (WebSearch plus OpenAlex) found the paper's versions v1 to v6 (May 2023 to Feb 2024) but no independent multilingual replication with other models, tasks or translation-quality controls. Related but not the same: a 2026 cross-cultural LLM risk-preference study exists (not opened), and a 2026 arXiv study varies user COUNTRY, not language (d21).
numbers: 0 replications found in 3 targeted searches.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search. Gap 2 stays open.
agent_relevance: Treat language-conditioned LLM preference gaps as unreplicated.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Under the Shadow of Babel, BICAUSE, Table 1 (400 samples)
finding: Table 1 accuracy by model, English vs Chinese. Chinese is not systematically worse. Llama-3.2-3B scores much higher in Chinese than English.
numbers: Average accuracy En vs Zh: Llama-3.2-1B 61.0 vs 49.8; Llama-3.2-3B 27.0 vs 56.8; Mistral-7B 95.8 vs 88.5; Qwen1.5-1.8B 91.0 vs 91.2; Qwen1.5-7B 93.2 vs 93.5; Qwen1.5-14B 96.8 vs 96.0; Qwen1.5-32B 92.8 vs 91.8; Qwen1.5-72B 95.5 vs 92.2. 8 domains x 50 samples = 400 per language.
limits: One lab. Model families differ in training mix and no data-mix control is run, so language effect and data effect are not separated (gap 3). The PDF's own caption for Table 1 is the plain accuracy table.
agent_relevance: Small-model language gaps are large and erratic; large Qwen models close the gap.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Under the Shadow of Babel, Table 2 (caption: paraphrased data)
finding: Second table. The Chinese deficit is clear in Qwen1.5-1.8B and Mistral-7B but absent in Qwen1.5-14B and 72B and reversed in 32B. This answers gap 3 in part: the gap does not hold uniformly above 7B within the Qwen family, but it does appear in Mistral-7B, a model not built around Chinese.
numbers: Average accuracy En vs Zh: Qwen1.5-1.8B 88.5 vs 76.8; Mistral-7B 93.8 vs 81.5 (gap 12.3); Llama-3.2-1B 53.2 vs 53.2; Llama-3.2-3B 63.8 vs 61.8; Qwen1.5-14B 97.5 vs 97.5; Qwen1.5-32B 90.5 vs 94.0; Qwen1.5-72B 97.0 vs 96.2.
limits: The PDF caption says Table 2 is paraphrased data, while earlier notes (b22) called this the reversed-order set; check the label before citing. Per-cell N is 50. No model above 72B, no frontier models. Data mix not controlled.
agent_relevance: A scaffold cannot assume the working language is neutral for small models; for large models the effect mostly vanishes in this test.

source: Zhang and Rayz (2026) Structured yet Bounded Temporal Understanding in Large Language Models (arXiv 2510.16685v2)
finding: Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B judge similarity between real-world events under a deictic frame (past-present-future) and a sequential frame (before-after). Under deictic framing similarity is graded and asymmetric: it falls sharply for future events and declines more gradually for past ones, and long past events are rated more similar than short ones. The duration effect does not appear for future events or in the sequential frame.
numbers: 2,916,927 data entries for the deictic frame and 51,360 for the sequential frame. Models generate at most 64 tokens. No effect sizes, CIs or significance tests in the text; results are plots of mean similarity vs distance and Allen interval relations.
limits: English only; the authors list other languages as future work, so the asymmetry has not been tested across languages (gap 9 stays open). Two models of one family.
agent_relevance: Wording frame (deictic vs sequential) changes LLM time judgements structurally, supporting 'state the time frame explicitly in prompts'.

source: Marjieh, Sucholutsky, van Rijn, Jacoby, Griffiths (2024) Large language models predict human sensory judgments across six modalities, Sci Reports 14:21445 (pitch part)
finding: GPT models predict human pairwise pitch similarity very well and recover the pitch spiral with a peak at 12 semitones (octave equivalence). The paper does not test height vs thickness pitch metaphors and does not vary prompt language for pitch, so gap 6 is not answered.
numbers: Pitch r=.92 (95% CI .91-.92, GPT-4); loudness r=.89 (GPT-3.5); colours r=.84 (GPT-4); consonants .57; taste .54; timbre .42. 55 human participants did the pitch task. With frequencies jittered by +-0.1 semitone: r=.86 GPT-3, .89 GPT-3.5, .95 GPT-4.
limits: One language (English) for pitch. Tones are C4-C6 only. LLM could recall MIDI knowledge, partly controlled by the jitter.
agent_relevance: Pitch knowledge is strong in text; no evidence that metaphor wording (high/low vs thick/thin) shifts it.

source: Marjieh et al. (2024) multilingual colour-naming experiment (English vs Russian), same Sci Reports paper
finding: Forced-choice naming of 330 Munsell chips from 15 names. GPT-4 is more human-like than GPT-3.5 and GPT-3 in both languages. The same hex codes led to different colour partitions in Russian and English prompts, which the authors read as consistent with either language distorting perceptual representation or just different name mappings on one perceptual space. No Winawer-style discrimination test was run on the model.
numbers: Adjusted Rand index vs humans: English GPT-4 0.59 (CI .56-.63), GPT-3.5 0.50, GPT-3 0.39; Russian GPT-4 0.54, GPT-3.5 0.50, GPT-3 0.35; lab ceiling 0.73 constrained / 0.75 free naming (Lindsey and Brown). Humans: 103 English, 51 Russian speakers.
limits: Naming is not discrimination: the Winawer category advantage is a speed effect that this task cannot show. GPT-4 naming dropped when given CIELAB/CIELUV codes instead of hex.
agent_relevance: Prompt language changes the colour categories the model applies, as a vocabulary effect. That is the weak, expected kind of language effect.

source: Loyola, Marrese-Taylor, Hoyos-Idrobo (2026) Probing the Geometry of Color Representations in Multilingual Language Models (arXiv 2610.18331)
finding: Layerwise embeddings of Gemma-2, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B and PaliGemma2 on colour terms in 10 languages (Many Languages Many Colors data). Alignment to CIELAB is weak and peaks in middle layers; cross-lingual symmetry is highest early and falls with depth. They conclude the models learn a universal colour-LANGUAGE geometry, not a universal colour-PERCEPTION geometry.
numbers: Cross-language congruence at layer 0 averages 0.61-0.71; final layers 0.29-0.56 (Llama-8B 0.56, Gemma-2B 0.30). 96.7% colour classification accuracy at the layer where perceptual alignment peaks; alignment correlates with downstream capability r=0.70.
limits: No Russian blue test. Representation-level probe, not a behavioural Whorf test.
agent_relevance: Language-specific structure grows with depth, so late-layer behaviour may differ by prompt language.

source: Wang, R. (2026) Do Multilingual Models Represent Colour Differently Across Languages? The Gap Is in the Vocabularies (ORACLE workshop at ACL, pp 476-483)
finding: Apparent cross-language differences in colour alignment (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) are largely produced by how colour words are spelled: where a term spells out its category (Chinese fenhong, German Feuerrot) a model can score well from spelling alone. On a shared set of 43 colours the four languages become too close to separate at that sample size.
numbers: Share of terms whose spelling names their category: 0% to 92% across four lexicons. Score share lost when spelling similarity is removed correlates r=0.84 with that share: 0-5% in Spanish and English, 32-71% in Chinese, 37-42% in German. On the raw test Chinese beats English; after removing spelling, English leads.
limits: Four languages, two models, no Russian. Small colour set (43).
agent_relevance: A caution: LLM cross-language differences can be artifacts of the lexicon, so any Whorf-style LLM test needs vocabulary controls.

source: Linguistic Relativity Meets Large Language Models: Does Prompting in Yoruba Elicit Qualitatively Different AI Outputs Than Prompting in English? (Zenodo preprint 2026)
finding: Claude Sonnet 4 answered 10 paired prompts on rural electrification in English and Yoruba. Yoruba outputs scored higher on a home-made cultural grounding index and lower on abstractness. The author calls this soft linguistic relativity.
numbers: Cultural grounding SGI 0.795 (Yoruba) vs 0.128 (English), t(9)=-8.41, Cohen's d=-3.999 (reported as +521%); abstractness ratio 0.287 vs 0.761, t(9)=13.13, d=6.846. n=10 prompt pairs, one model, temperature 1.0.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed, novel unvalidated metrics, one model, n=10, answers about local culture where a content difference is expected. A topic and training-data effect, not a Whorf effect on a nonlinguistic task.
agent_relevance: Prompt language changes what the model brings up. Not evidence about reasoning quality.

source: Jehu-Appiah (2026) Umwelt Engineering: Designing the Cognitive Worlds of Linguistic Agents (arXiv 2603.27626)
finding: Tests a vocabulary-restriction version of linguistic relativity on LLM agents. Exp 1: Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4o-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite reasoned under No-Have (no possessive 'to have') or E-Prime (no 'to be'). Effects are task and model dependent. Exp 2: 16 agents with different linguistic constraints on 17 debugging problems; none beat the control alone, but a 3-agent diverse ensemble covered more.
numbers: N=4,470 trials, 7 tasks. No-Have: ethical reasoning +19.1 pp (p<0.001), classification +6.5 pp, epistemic calibration +7.4 pp, 92.8% compliance. E-Prime: causal +14.1 pp, ethics +15.5 pp; Gemini ethics +42.3 pp but GPT-4o-mini calibration -27.5 pp; cross-model correlation r=-0.75. Exp 2: 3-agent ensemble 100% ground-truth coverage vs 88.2% control; 8% of random 3-agent subsets reach full coverage.
limits: Preprint, small models, single author, no active control matching constraint-prompt length (the author says so). Constraints also cut verbosity (the most robust effect), which confounds accuracy. E-Prime violation rate was 51.9%.
agent_relevance: The only study found that manipulates the linguistic medium of an agent and measures reasoning. Suggests language constraint as a diversity lever across ensemble members, not as a general boost.

source: Pratim Ray (2025) Does Linguistic Relativity Hypothesis Apply on ChatGPT Responses? Yes, It Does (as cited by the Yoruba paper)
finding: Known only from the Yoruba paper's description: ChatGPT outputs in different languages frame the same query with different epistemological orientations. A separate OpenAlex hit, 'Challenges and Verification: The Reproduction of the Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis by Large Language Models' (2025), was found but its PDF did not download.
numbers: No numbers recovered.
limits: Second-hand. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Same as d17.

source: Search note: LLM tests of ego-moving vs time-moving framing and of the space-time asymmetry
finding: Three WebSearch queries and about 18 OpenAlex queries found no study that gives an LLM the Next-Wednesday-meeting ambiguous question under spatial primes, none that tests whether length cues distort LLM duration estimates more than the reverse, and none on height vs thickness pitch wording. Closest items: Zhang and Rayz 2026 (d12), Gurnee and Tegmark (a23), Marjieh (d13). A human replication of the meeting question with 599 participants (from a search summary, not opened) reportedly found only the time-moving prime worked.
numbers: 0 direct LLM studies found for gaps 1 and 10; one search-summary mention of a human N=599 replication.
limits: Search limited by API rate limits (Semantic Scholar 429) and an empty arXiv API response, so a miss is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: These tests remain a gap and would be cheap to run.

source: He, Reusens, Goethals, Martens (2026) A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time (arXiv 2610.18515)
finding: Varies only the user's country (193 countries, 5 LLMs) and measures the compensation LLMs consider fair for a 60-minute delay. LLMs recommend the highest compensation for Europe and mostly the lowest for Africa. It varies country, not prompt language.
numbers: 193 countries, 5 LLMs; compared with GDP PPP, mean income and a Patience Score. No effect sizes extracted.
limits: Not a Whorf test; recorded to show the nearest 'time preference' LLM study does not vary language.
agent_relevance: Time preference in LLMs is driven by stereotyped country cues, a warning against reading language effects off such tasks.
